design_detail: Historical narrative review (Drug Science, Policy and Law, vol. 4, published online 11 April 2018; free access on the SAGE site) of the use of MDMA in psychotherapy in the United States from 1977 to 1985, when it was legal and unscheduled, and of the scheduling process, by a single author, a psychiatrist and historian of psychedelic therapy. Sources: memoirs and books by early practitioners and their associates (for example Stolaroff, 2004; Shulgin and Shulgin), conference reports, a self-published and later journal-published follow-up of patients (Greer and Tolbert, 1986), an unpublished study (Kueny, 1980), an informal therapist survey (ARUPA, 1984), an unapproved physiological study (Downing, 1986), court records, press reports, interviews and personal communications. No search strategy, no appraisal of the cited reports, no quantitative synthesis. Also describes session practices and guidelines of the period, which this card does not reproduce.
can_establish: Who used MDMA in psychotherapy before it was scheduled, in what settings and with what stated aims, what early reports and testimonies claimed, how the 1984 to 1988 scheduling unfolded, and which abuses by therapists were documented.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted psychotherapy helped or harmed patients in that period: the outcome evidence described is uncontrolled reports, testimonies and one small follow-up, relayed without appraisal; the numbers of people treated come from memoirs, interviews and the author's own extrapolation.

sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated; the author's selection of sources.
sample.selection_effects: Sources are mostly practitioners, advocates and their circles (the Boston group, ARUPA, EMDL, MAPS founders); regulators' and critics' positions are given briefly; some figures rest on personal communications with more than 10 informants.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable; the review describes therapeutic practices of the period in prose.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Doses of the period are mentioned in the article; not reproduced here.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The only outcome figures described: Greer and Tolbert's follow-up of 29 patients (no serious side effects or negative after-effects found; 23 reported positive changes in attitude lasting from 1 week to the 2-year follow-up), and an informal survey in which 15 of 16 therapists judged MDMA valuable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable; the review relays proponents' accounts of benefit and safety without appraisal, while also documenting two cases of sexual abuse by therapists.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A history: a few dozen US therapists used MDMA in psychotherapy between about 1977 and 1985, with caseloads reported in memoirs and interviews; outcome evidence consisted of uncontrolled reports and testimonies; two therapists sexually abused patients during MDMA sessions; the DEA's administrative law judge recommended against Schedule I, the DEA overruled him, and research applications were then blocked until 1992.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls MDMA's properties "benign, feeling-enhancing, and nonhallucinatory" and says the pioneers laid the groundwork for later studies; the review states that the safety profile was very good overall and side effects all mild, judgments that rest on practitioners' reports rather than on studies able to detect harms. The estimate of more than 60,000 people treated underground from 1985 to 2017 is the author's extrapolation from informants, presented with caveats.

timeline.event: 27 July 1984: the DEA proposes placing MDMA in Schedule I; therapists and EMDL request a hearing (per this review).
Hearings; the administrative law judge recommends against Schedule I and the DEA overrules him; the WHO Expert Committee recommends international control while urging research (per this review).
Greer and Tolbert publish their follow-up of 29 patients (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs), the main outcome report of the period (not read).
The 'Grinspoon window' (22 December 1987 to 22 March 1988) closes; the DEA holds that accepted medical use requires FDA approval (per this review).
The first FDA-approved study of MDMA in humans begins, in healthy volunteers, after earlier applications were placed on clinical hold (per this review).
Long-term follow-up of the first randomized trial of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD.

replication.where_it_stands: A useful historical account by one author, consistent in outline with the 1985 to 1986 primary documents on the project's list (not read here). Claims about the history may cite it as a narrative review; claims about efficacy or safety in that period should not.

funding.funder: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication.
funding.declared_conflicts: The author declared no potential conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: The author has written several histories of MDMA and psycholytic therapy, some with Benzenhöfer, which this review cites for background.

what_would_settle_it: For the history: the primary documents of 1985 to 1986 (the hearing record, the judge's recommended ruling, the WHO committee report, the early clinical papers) read directly. For the clinical question the history raises: controlled trials, which began only in the 2000s.

domains.note: No search or selection criteria; sources chosen by the author, many of them memoirs, interviews and personal communications.
Uncontrolled reports and therapists' testimonies of benefit and safety are relayed without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The author's earlier histories are cited for background, not as evidence of effects.
The underground-treatment estimate is labelled as such, but judgments of safety and benefit are stated as findings.

domains.domain: Balance of the history (regulators' and critics' views of the early claims are under-represented)
domains.note: Documents the abuse cases and the WHO's methodological reservation, but presents the case for therapeutic use mainly through its proponents; the DEA's and FDA's reasoning is summarized in a sentence or two.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3). As history the review is informative and dated; as evidence about effects it is second-hand and unappraised. Cite it for who did what and when, and for the scheduling sequence it describes; any claim resting only on it stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: A few dozen psychotherapists, mostly in California and elsewhere on the West Coast, used MDMA in psychotherapy between about 1977 and 1985, when it was neither an FDA-approved drug nor a controlled substance; in California and some other states a physician could use it legally if self-synthesized, with informed consent and a peer-reviewed protocol.
key_findings.note: The abstract and title say 1977, the Discussion 1978.

key_findings.finding: Reported caseloads (from memoirs, interviews and the practitioners' own accounts): Leo Zeff gave MDMA to about 4000 people over 12 years and trained more than 150 therapists (Stolaroff, 2004); George Greer and Requa Tolbert treated more than 80 patients from 1980 to 1985; Rick Ingrasci 100 patients in about 150 sessions, one-third with couples, including 11 people with cancer; Claudio Naranjo more than 30 patients by 1984; Deborah Harlow more than 200 clients before 1985.
key_findings.locator: Leo Zeff—The Secret Chief, 2nd paragraph; George Greer's work with MDMA in psychotherapy, 1st paragraph; Rick Ingrasci: MDMA in couples and patients with life-threatening illnesses, 1st and 6th paragraphs; Claudio Naranjo, 2nd paragraph; A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The main outcome report described is Greer and Tolbert's follow-up of 29 patients (self-published 1983, published 1986): no serious side effects or negative after-effects were found, and 23 reported positive changes in attitude lasting between 1 week and the follow-up time of 2 years; there was no comparison group.
key_findings.locator: George Greer's work with MDMA in psychotherapy, 5th paragraph (author's paragraphs; block quotations not counted)

key_findings.finding: Other early evidence: an unpublished exploratory study of nine people given one MDMA session each (Kueny, 1980); a 1984 survey of 16 therapists for ARUPA, in which 15 judged MDMA valuable in augmenting psychotherapy and all claimed negligible complications and low abuse potential, used as evidence at the hearings; and a 1984 study of 21 people with prior MDMA experience, run without FDA or institutional review board approval, reporting dose-dependent rises in blood pressure of 20 to 40 mm Hg and no complications.
key_findings.locator: Kueny's 1980 study, 1st paragraph; A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; The first psychophysiological study of MDMA in humans, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Two therapists, Rick Ingrasci and Francesco DiLeo, initiated sexual contact and intercourse with patients during MDMA sessions; both were sued and lost their licences; DiLeo's patient was later diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety and awarded damages by a Maryland court (1991). According to Harlow, the Ingrasci case led to the rule of male-female co-therapist teams in later studies.
key_findings.locator: Physical abuse in MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Scheduling: on 27 July 1984 the DEA recommended Schedule I; a hearing was requested and held in 1985; the administrative law judge concluded that MDMA did not have to be placed in Schedule I (therapeutic potential, could be handled without grave dangers under medical supervision, no high abuse potential, not proven toxic in humans); the DEA overruled him; an appeal suspended the scheduling from 22 December 1987 to 22 March 1988, after which the DEA held that accepted medical use requires FDA approval.
key_findings.locator: Therapists opposed to the scheduling of MDMA in 1985, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, which recommended international control of MDMA in late 1985, found the reports of therapeutic usefulness intriguing but methodologically inadequate and urged countries to facilitate research (WHO, 1985).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs (the WHO statement is a block quotation)

key_findings.finding: After scheduling, five applications to the FDA to study MDMA (1986 to 1988) were placed on clinical hold on grounds of possible neurotoxicity; a protocol for anxiety in terminal cancer was rejected in 1992; the first FDA-approved MDMA study in humans, in healthy volunteers, began in 1992. In Switzerland, five members of a physicians' society were permitted to use MDMA and LSD in psychotherapy from 1988 to 1993.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph; MDMA therapy goes underground, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The indications explored by the early therapists (trauma, anxiety associated with terminal cancer, psychoneuroses and couples) were also those taken up in later research.
key_findings.locator: Indications, precautions, and session guidelines, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The author estimates, from more than 10 informants and assumed session numbers, that more than 60,000 people may have been treated with MDMA in underground therapy from 1985 to 2017, an estimate he calls probably conservative and that cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The start of the period is 1977 in the title and abstract and 1978 in the Discussion; the section on underground therapy says European work began in the late 1970s, before scheduling, under a heading about going underground after it.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Title; Abstract; Discussion, 1st paragraph; MDMA therapy goes underground, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; dates in a history claim should be given as 'from the late 1970s'.
